Hello,

Sadly I wasn't able to attend the rally at Berkeley, but I went to a pro-Trump rally that day in the Rio Grande Valley, which is at the tip of south Texas for those who aren't familiar.

As you might imagine this was much more quiet than the other big rallies. It was held at the office of the open-borders Democrat congressman in the area. I wasn't sure what to expect, but since I helped organize for Trump down here before the election people mostly knew who I was.

I showed up with a custom Pepe flag which got a lot of attention. There was a significant Tea Party presence, which I found surprising because most of the Tea Party here was adamantly pro-Cruz and refused to help the Trump campaign during the general election. I was not interested in speaking to those people, as they weren't there when we needed them.

Someone I did not recognized shouted that "we memed a president into existence!" Pepe got a lot of attention, first from older people who had no clue what Pepe was. I explained to them as best as I could the memes, getting Trump trending on Twitter, and how the Clinton campaign tried to paint it as "white supremacist." Most of the older folks seemed to buy my explanation. I don't know whether most people here are friendly the alt-right or not and I don't know what preconceptions they may have. The clear majority of pro-Trump people down here are Hispanic.

There were a couple of speeches given from the back of a pickup truck. One was from a Hispanic police officer who said that it was the first time in his life that his family and friends called him "racist" for supporting Trump. That was amusing. There was another speech given by the local Tea Party leader, an older white man. I found this even more amusing because after the primaries this person was adamant in NOT lifting a finger to help Trump. Now that Trump had won, he seems to have changed his tune. Fair weather friends.

After the speech one younger Mexican-looking woman in her 20s confronted me about Pepe meaning "white, white supremacy." I accused her of regurgitating talking points from the Hillary Clinton campaign. She pressed me for the meaning of Pepe and I gave her the same shtick I did the others, then turned my back and ignored her. I regret being so nice. In any case it didn't matter.

A lot of younger people wanted to take pictures with me and the Pepe flag; all of them millennial and Hispanic. I think I took three pictures with folks posing with the Pepe flag, including a picture with two siblings with Mexican national accents and upper-class Mexican mannerisms (if you've live down here long enough you notice the difference between Mexican and 'Texican.')

I'm not the type of person who looks to non-white people to justify myself, however, if they are enthusiastic and friendly to me of course I am going to reciprocate that and be friends with them. I was quite surprised to see how well-received I was there, and how many of the younger people recognized what I was doing immediately.

I put up a short video of the rally on my Facebook page if anyone is interested. It was a quiet rally and there were no troubles at all. Not nearly as exciting as Berkeley, but insightful in its own right.
